lesson.menu_title: The Art of Small Talk — The Table You Never Sat At
lesson.menu_desc: A dinner in Sao Paulo, an Italian architect and the story you almost did not tell -- 36 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 2 -- The Art of Small Talk
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Braulio Zemel | Lesson 2 -- The Art of Small Talk

listenings.text: Braulio, hi, it is Renata, Marina gave me your number. Listen, we are having a few people over on Saturday, about eight o'clock, and Marina said you might both come. It is nothing formal. There will be nine of us, and three of them are visiting from Lisbon, so most of the evening will be in English. I know Marina said you have been studying, so I thought I would tell you in advance instead of surprising you at the door. Bring nothing. Just come. Call me back when you can and let me know.

People complain that small talk is empty, and in one sense they are right. Nobody at a dinner table genuinely needs to know whether it rained this afternoon. But that is not what the question is for. The weather is a test signal. It says: I am open, I am friendly, and I am willing to spend thirty seconds on nothing in order to find out whether we have anything else. Researchers who study first conversations found that the topic almost never matters. What matters is the second question. Anybody can answer once. The person who asks you something back is the person who wants the conversation. So if you take one thing from this programme, take that. Do not worry about your opening line. Worry about your second question.

extra_audio.text: Elena introduces herself and admits she has been rehearsing something to say for two courses. Braulio tells her his name and asks what she was rehearsing. She says it was about the weather, and asks where he is from. He answers Sao Paulo, and mentions the house in Bahia and the ten days a month. Elena says she is from Milan and has been in Sao Paulo for eleven years, and the two of them find common ground in the news.

paras: For about fifteen years I was the quiet one at dinner. My wife is Danish and her English is better than mine has ever been, so at every table abroad she talked and I ate. People thought I was serious. I was not serious. I was tongue-tied.

What changed was not a course. It was one evening in Lisbon, when a man across the table picked up on something I had said about the price of housing and asked me a direct question about it. I answered in five words. He asked another. Twenty minutes later we were still going. If he had not asked that second question, I would have gone home the same man I arrived as.

Since then I have paid attention to how it actually works, and it is less impressive than people think. Somebody breaks the ice with something small and slightly boring. Somebody else brings up a subject with a little weight in it. Then two people find common ground, and the rest of the table relaxes. Small talk is not the opposite of real conversation. It is the corridor you walk down to reach it.

The part I got wrong for fifteen years was thinking I had to be fluent to join in. I did not. I had to be curious out loud. If I had understood that at forty, I would have had fifteen more years of dinners instead of fifteen years of nodding politely and looking at my plate.
